title: The banyan seed
hookLine: break a seed, see nothing, and learn what holds up the whole tree
carry: the unseen essence holds up the world
last: THE TREE — THE BODY DIES. THE SELF DOES NOT.

lines: A TREE THAT LOOKS LIKE A FOREST.
IT STARTED AS A TINY SEED.
cards: A banyan doesn't stop at one trunk. It sends roots down from its branches, and those roots thicken into new trunks, until one tree can look like a small forest.
Birds nest in it, people sit in its shade, and all of it is one tree. Its fruit is a little fig a bird could swallow whole, with seeds like specks of dust inside. Uddalaka sends his son to fetch one.

teach.h: BREAK THE FRUIT. BREAK THE SEED.
teach.b: The lesson is a short conversation, almost a game. Bring me a fruit from that banyan. Here it is, sir.

teach.h: WHAT DO YOU SEE? NOTHING AT ALL.
teach.b: What do you see? These tiny seeds, sir. Break one of them.
It's broken, sir. What do you see there? Nothing at all, sir.
And the father says: my dear, that subtle essence you can't see, from that very essence this great banyan tree stands. Believe me, my dear. He doesn't describe the seed.
He has his son break it with his own hands and look, and the son reports honestly: nothing. That nothing is the point. Not empty nothing.
Uddalaka's word is anima, the subtlest. Here is the Hindu teaching: what's most real isn't the biggest thing in the room. It's the unseen essence that everything you can see stands on.
Then he asks for shraddha, faith: shraddhatsva, believe me. Not belief instead of looking; his son has just looked as hard as anyone can.
In this story, faith comes after looking, at the edge of what eyes can do. So when a classmate asks, where's God, under a microscope? Uddalaka's son already tried that with a seed.
Look as closely as you like. The tree is still standing.
Then the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this world. You are that, Shvetaketu.

how: The banyan is sacred to many Hindus and is often worshipped, especially by women during the Vat Savitri festival; teachers use Uddalaka's banyan seed to explain the subtle essence behind the visible world.

o: the seed of a tree planted at a temple
the subtlest essence, too fine to be seen
the breath of life that leaves at death

games.q: what's inside the lesson — tap the pairs.

s: Uddalaka describes the seed instead of showing it
he has his son break the fruit and the seed with his own hands, and look.
inside the broken seed, Shvetaketu sees nothing at all
that unseen subtle essence is where the great tree comes from.
Uddalaka asks his son to believe instead of looking
he asks for faith only after the son has looked as hard as he can.

games.q: Uddalaka asks his son to have faith, shraddha, in what he can't see. when does he ask?
o: before the son looks, so he won't need to.
after the son has broken the seed and looked as hard as he can.
never: the Upanishads don't speak of faith.
games.why: break the fruit, break the seed, look: nothing. only then, believe me, my dear. faith comes after looking, at the edge of seeing.

practice: Start with something big in your life, your body, your family, your work, and go smaller, the way the son broke the fruit and then the seed: what's this made of, and that?
When you reach the edge of what you can see, don't force an answer; rest there.

wordCard.voice: Anima, the subtlest, the finest. Broken open, the banyan seed shows nothing at all; from that unseen, subtle essence, the father says, the great banyan stands.

orig.note: Sanskrit aṇimā: subtleness, the finest essence. sa ya eṣo 'ṇimā: that which is this subtle essence.

carryVoice: Your line: the unseen essence holds up the world. From that, this great tree stands. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.12.1–3 (the banyan fruit; anima; shraddhatsva; the refrain)
